article.overview: Molten regolith electrolysis (MRE) is an in-situ resource utilisation (ISRU) process that melts lunar soil, known as regolith, and passes an electric current through the melt so that oxygen is released and metals are left behind [1][2]. A demonstrator is a payload built to test this process at a useful scale and in a space-like environment, rather than only in a laboratory bench test. The most advanced public demonstration reviewed for this article is a late-2024 ground test at NASA Kennedy Space Center (KSC) of a Lunar Resources Inc. LR-1 reactor. The test processed 25 kg of regolith simulant in a vacuum chamber and averaged 0.07 kg of oxygen per hour over nine hours of electrolysis [1][2]. Other demonstrator concepts, including the Airbus-led Mini-ROXY payload and an ESA-sponsored payload study led by Thales Alenia Space UK, use related but different processes and have no confirmed flight date [5][6][7][8]. No MRE demonstrator has been shown to operate on the Moon in the sources reviewed.
article.description: A molten regolith electrolysis demonstrator tests a process in which lunar regolith, the loose layer of broken rock and glass that covers the Moon, is heated until it melts. In the melt, oxygen that is chemically bound in the minerals can be removed by electrolysis: electric current flows through the liquid, oxygen-bearing ions give up their electrons at an anode, and the oxygen escapes as gas. Metal ions in the melt gain electrons at a cathode and form liquid metal or metal alloys [2]. Because the regolith itself acts as the electrolyte, MRE does not need a separate salt bath. A demonstrator is designed to show the whole chain working together: heating, melt control, gas release, oxygen measurement and product handling. In the 2024 KSC test the melt was sustained partly by Joule heating, meaning heat generated by the resistance of the molten material to the electric current [1][2]. A demonstrator is therefore both a chemical reactor and a test of thermal and power management.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of an MRE demonstrator is to show that oxygen can be produced from real or simulated regolith at a scale and under conditions that matter for a lunar base. NASA's KSC team describes the 2024 test as a ground demonstration of a commercially developed MRE reactor, intended to measure its oxygen-production performance in a 1 g vacuum environment and to capture lessons for future maturation [2]. Measurements in such tests include the oxygen production rate, the composition of the evolved gas, the temperature history of the melt and the chemistry of the reduced regolith after the run [1][2]. The oxygen could serve as breathing air or as oxidiser for rocket propellant, and the metals could be used in manufacturing, including solar panels, according to NASA's public description [4]. Mini-ROXY, a related molten-salt concept, aims to demonstrate oxygen extraction from regolith with process diagnostics that measure oxygen flow and purity, and to characterise the process [5][6]. The ESA-sponsored payload study targets 50 to 100 g of oxygen from regolith with precise gas-concentration measurements [8]. Metal production and other applications are discussed by the developers but have not been demonstrated at lunar scale [2][4].
article.operating_principle: The melt acts as both electrolyte and feedstock. The NASA slides summarise the anode reaction as 2O2- (in the melt) to O2 (gas) + 4 e-, and the cathode reduction of metal cations such as Si4+ to molten silicon, with each oxygen molecule requiring four electrons [2]. The total electrical current therefore limits the maximum possible oxygen production rate [2]. The slides describe a regolith heating phase to about 1400 degrees C, a melt of about 1600 degrees C, and Joule heating maintaining high temperatures during electrolysis [2]. The 2024 test used an electrolysis setpoint of 45 V with an overall current of 210 A [2]. Oxygen leaves the reactor as a gas, which is measured by a gas-analysis system (the VMOMS system) that identifies gases during evacuation, heating and electrolysis [2]. Because the process needs a molten charge, the main engineering issues are thermal insulation, containment of the melt, controlled gas outlets, and handling of the solidified residue after each run [1][2].
article.scientific_importance: The Moon's surface is a possible source of oxygen, metals and other materials. Producing oxygen from regolith would reduce the need to launch breathing gas or propellant oxidiser from Earth, which is why NASA's stated aim is to mature this technology for long-duration lunar presence [2][4]. MRE is scientifically interesting because it processes the whole regolith: the same electrical process that releases oxygen also reduces metal oxides to metals and semi-metals, such as silicon [2]. NASA notes that the metals could be used in solar panels [4]. The process has a long research history, from a 1990 magma-electrolysis concept to electrode and reactor-modelling studies and to the present test at KSC [2]. The 2024 test is significant because it moved MRE from small laboratory samples to a 25 kg batch inside a vacuum test environment, although it remained a ground test with simulant rather than lunar soil [1][2].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for an MRE demonstrator. The sources reviewed describe a ground-test reactor (LR-1), a proposed lunar demonstrator (Mini-ROXY, which uses a related molten-salt process) and an ESA payload study with performance targets but no published hardware dimensions. The LR-1 mass and dimensions are not publicly stated in the sources reviewed. Where a figure is a design target or a slide annotation, it is labelled as such.

electrical_setpoint.note: Overall setpoint stated on NASA slides. The product of these values is about 9.5 kW; the slides separately state a maximum power draw of about 9 kW during vacuum chamber operations.

oxygen_production_rate_kg_per_hr.conditions: Average over the electrolysis run under vacuum conditions

oxygen_concentration_by_volume_percent.note: Several gas-measurement data points reported up to 80 percent molecular oxygen by volume

reported_produced_oxygen_weight_percent.note: Appears on NASA slides without a stated basis; not interpreted in this article

temperature_c.heating_stage: Heated to about 1300 C, with thermal conditioning at 1200 to 1300 C
temperature_c.melt_during_test: Slides describe melt temperatures from about 1400 to 1600 C and temperatures above 1700 C under Joule heating. The NASA public article gives a melting temperature of 1700 C (3,100 F).

test_chamber.name: ASSIST (Atmospherically Sealed Simulator for In-situ System Testing)

examples.post_test_analysis: Computed tomography, X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy and energy-dispersive spectroscopy on a core sample of the reduced melt
examples.qualification: Ground test in vacuum at 1 g (Earth gravity) using simulant. Not a flight qualification and not a lunar-gravity test.

consortium.member_roles: Not stated for individual members in the ESA announcement

examples.measurement_requirement: Precise measurements of performance and gas concentrations
examples.description_as_stated: Described as a small, compact, low-power piece of equipment

examples.name: Mars Oxygen In-Situ Resource Utilization Experiment (MOXIE)
examples.type: Flown technology demonstration on NASA's Perseverance rover on Mars. A different process (electrolysis of carbon dioxide from the Martian atmosphere), not molten regolith electrolysis; included only as a flown ISRU comparator.
examples.size_description: Described as the size of a lunchbox in the MIT AeroAstro article
examples.results: First oxygen run in April 2021. By the end of 2021, seven experimental runs had been completed, and each reached the 6 g per hour target. Cumulative totals and purity figures are not given in the source reviewed.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No verified dimensions are published for the LR-1 reactor in the sources reviewed. The ASSIST chamber used for the 2024 test has a test volume of 1.4 by 1.1 by 1.4 m, which is a test-facility dimension and not a reactor dimension. The Mini-ROXY slide annotations of about 30 cm and 50 cm are not attributed to a specific dimension. A future MRE demonstrator's size would depend on its melt volume, insulation, cooling, power and gas-handling systems.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The only published demonstrator mass in this set is the approximately 30 kg Mini-ROXY slide annotation, which is a concept figure. The LR-1 test reactor mass is not stated. The 25 kg figure refers to the regolith simulant batch, not to the reactor. Mass is a major constraint for landers, so a flight demonstrator would need a verified mass budget before any compatibility claim.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The 2024 LR-1 ground test had an overall electrolysis setpoint of 45 V and 210 A, with a stated maximum power draw of about 9 kW during vacuum chamber operations [2]. Joule heating contributed to sustaining the melt [1][2]. A flight demonstrator's power requirement and its power source (solar, battery or lander supply) are not stated in the sources reviewed; the ESA payload is described as low power, and the Mini-ROXY concept is described as flexible through thermal insulation [5][8].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: An MRE demonstrator must operate in vacuum, with no atmosphere to carry heat away from hot surfaces and no air to supply combustion-free gas handling. The 2024 KSC test used a vacuum chamber, a test pressure of 9.84E-06 Torr on the ASSIST chamber and 0.8 Torr on the LR-1 reactor during leak checks [2]. The reactor operated at temperatures above 1700 C under Joule heating, so thermal design, shielding of seals and safe external temperatures were central. NASA's thermal modelling led to a front deflector shield on the test door to protect door seals, and supplementary cooling fans were added to make the exterior safe to touch [2]. Ground tests were performed at Earth gravity (1 g), so gas bubbling, melt behaviour and dust behaviour in lunar gravity were not tested in those tests. Mini-ROXY developers state that their process avoids gas bubbling in low gravity because the oxygen passes through a solid oxide membrane, but this is a developer claim and not a test result [5]. A lunar surface demonstrator would also need a power source for the duration of its operating window, and the ESA payload is described as operating within one lunar day [8].
article.limitations: The 2024 demonstration used regolith simulant, not lunar soil, and it was a ground test in a vacuum chamber at 1 g. Its measured oxygen rate, 0.07 kg per hour, is an average over a nine-hour run, and the NASA sources do not give the reactor mass, dimensions, or a verified power budget for a flight unit [1][2]. The reported 2.3 weight percent produced-oxygen figure has no stated basis in the sources. A single demonstrator would not by itself establish how an MRE plant behaves over multiple cycles or on a lunar regolith batch. The Mini-ROXY and ESA payload results are design targets and concept data, not measured lunar performance [5][8].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: No MRE demonstrator has a verified flight manifest in the sources reviewed. The LR-1 reactor was tested as a ground article. The Mini-ROXY concept and the ESA payload study both describe lunar surface operation, but neither source names a verified lander interface or launch date. This section therefore describes the transport and deployment steps that a surface demonstrator would need to address, rather than asserting a specific delivery plan.
transportation_process: Integrate the demonstrator into a lander or rover payload compartment on Earth, with its power, thermal and data interfaces defined for the chosen carrier.
Launch it toward the Moon on a launch vehicle, followed by lunar transfer and descent.

Land it with the carrier, where the lander provides the mechanical and power interface. Mini-ROXY is described as a robotic secondary payload that depends on external systems for power and data [5][6].
Deploy the reactor and external systems on a suitable surface and check thermal and gas-handling interfaces before operation.
Operate within the allowed window. Mini-ROXY is described with a lunar-day operating goal, and the ESA payload is described with a window within one lunar day [5][8].

After each run, allow the melt to cool and handle the solidified residue, and manage oxygen storage or venting as the mission design requires. Oxygen storage is not needed for a basic demonstration, according to the Mini-ROXY RFI [6].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: No deployment method has been verified for an MRE demonstrator. Mini-ROXY is intended as a payload on a lander or rover with external power and data systems, and the developers name NASA as a possible source of external elements [5][6]. Deployment design would depend on whether the demonstrator is fixed or mobile and on the mass and thermal constraints of the carrier.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The 2024 LR-1 test is a ground-based example, not a flight example. The MOXIE instrument, flown on Perseverance, shows a flown ISRU oxygen experiment on Mars, though it uses a different process and was not deployed by an MRE system [9].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lander compatibility is established for any MRE demonstrator in this article. The Mini-ROXY reference lander (Astrobotic Peregrine) is a 2024-era reference and has not been verified as current [5]. The ESA payload is described as designed for several landers, including EL3, but no interface document was reviewed [8]. Compatibility would need comparison of mass, dimensions, mounting, landing loads, power, thermal and data interfaces against a verified lander specification.

article.historical_significance: The MRE concept dates back to a 1990 magma-electrolysis study, and molten-regolith electrode and reactor-modelling work followed in 2009 and 2015 [2]. NASA's Swamp Works at Kennedy has developed molten regolith reactors since the early 1990s, and the GaLORE vacuum-based concept ran from 2019 to 2023 [4]. The December 2024 KSC test is described by NASA as the first time NASA had produced molecular oxygen with this process [4]. That statement is a NASA claim and is reported here as such. The ESA payload study, announced in March 2022, followed a competitive phase that compared three rival designs [8]. Mini-ROXY is a more recent demonstrator concept developed by Airbus and partners, with DLR funding, and its ILA 2026 exhibit shows a model [5][7].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The LR-1 measurements come from a ground test with simulant at Earth gravity. The full manuscript for the 2026 paper (NTRS 20260003760) was linked but not reviewed in full, so reactor mass, operating temperature, purity and power figures should be checked against that source before reuse [3]. The Mini-ROXY dimensions, mass and lander references are slide annotations or 2024-era material [5][6]. The ESA payload has no published mass, size, power or flight date [8]. The MOXIE comparator is a flown Mars instrument with a different process and is not a measure of MRE performance [9]. No value in this article should be read as a flight-qualified specification.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Image objects are repeated in section-level arrays where displayed. The Mini-ROXY image has image_url null because no direct asset was verified; its linked source page is used instead.

data_quality_notes: Most MRE figures come from NASA KSC ICES 2026 slides, extracted from a PDF with pdftotext. Values were read from slide text and were not checked against the full manuscript (NTRS 20260003760), which was not accessible as readable text.
The 2.3 weight percent produced-oxygen figure on the NASA slides has no stated basis and is not interpreted.
The LR-1 reactor mass, dimensions, power capability and operating temperature setpoints are not stated in the sources reviewed.
A 2024 NASA program review threshold (0.1 kg/h) and 14-hour target were seen only in a search-result summary and were not verified from a primary document; they are not used in the article.
The Metalysis process temperature (about 950 C in calcium chloride) appeared only in secondary press coverage and was not verified; it is not used in the article.
The Mini-ROXY 30 kg mass and 30 cm and 50 cm dimensions are slide annotations; the dimensions they refer to are not stated.
The Mini-ROXY reference lander (Astrobotic Peregrine) is from a 2024-era presentation and has not been verified as current.
The ESA payload has no published mass, size, power, process temperature or launch date. The ESA announcement is dated 9 March 2022 and describes a hardware development payload.
The MOXIE cumulative oxygen total seen in a search summary was not confirmed from a primary source and is excluded.
The NASA image URL returned a JPEG, but its picture content and caption were not visually confirmed; direct_image_assets_verified_from_official_pages is set to false.
The DLR image URL was reported on the source page but not fetched as a binary asset, so image_url is null.
Some search-result text contained formatting reminders addressed to the reader. They were treated as data and ignored.
